concept.name: Bull call spread
concept.definition: A bull call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate rise in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry.
concept.intuition: You buy upside participation but sell away the part above the higher strike to reduce the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.
concept.mechanics: Net debit = premium paid - premium received. Maximum loss is the debit (below the lower strike); maximum gain is (strike width - debit) at or above the higher strike. The CFTC describes the call bull spread as buying the lower-strike (higher-delta) call and selling the higher-strike call.
concept.formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K1 + net debit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
concept.failure_modes: The capped upside badly lags outright call or stock ownership in large rallies; early assignment on the short ITM leg (especially before ex-dividend) can disrupt the spread and create an unintended stock position.
concept.misconceptions: It is not 'free leverage': the reduced cost comes from selling the tail upside, and the probability-weighted expectancy still reflects the market's implied distribution. Limited risk does not mean likely profit.
concept.example: Buy the XYZ $100 call for $4, sell the $105 call for $1.50: debit $2.50. Above $105 the spread is worth $5, a $2.50 gain; below $100 the $250 debit is lost.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
